name: asar
desc: SNES assembler for applying patches to ROM images or building ROMs
why: An SNES assembler for patching ROMs opens a door into the ROM hacking scene and 65816 assembly.

brief.what_it_is: Asar is an SNES assembler for applying patches to existing ROM images or creating new ROM images from scratch. It supports the 65c816, SPC700, and Super FX architectures. You feed it assembly source (patch files) plus a ROM image, and it writes the assembled bytes into the ROM. The README does not spell out the exact output file behaviour; it says only that it can apply patches or build ROMs. Per the README, it was originally created by Alcaro and modelled after xkas v0.06 by byuu.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a tool for SNES patching and ROM creation, modelled on the older xkas assembler. The README is aimed at tool programmers and contributors, and the user guide lives in README.txt and the online manual.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internal mechanism. It mentions that Asar is built with CMake and can also be built as a DLL or a static library for embedding in other programs. Patch files can contain test lines written as ;` comments that check ROM bytes after patching, and the README says Asar uses multiple passes when assembling.

commands_seen.context: The README's basic Linux build from source, run from the repository root.
Generates the build project; on Windows you then open the generated project file in Visual Studio and click Build.
Adds Asar as a git submodule when embedding its static library in another project.

brief.install_notes: Build from source with CMake (cmake src && make on Linux; cmake src then Visual Studio on Windows), or download a prebuilt binary from the GitHub Releases page. The README.txt says that on Windows you can double-click asar.exe and it will prompt for the patch file and the ROM, while command-line arguments are documented in the manual. The Homebrew formula is a separate route not covered by these pages. The repo also ships syntax highlighting for Notepad++ and Sublime Text under ext/.
brief.standout: Asar is the SNES assembler that the ROM hacking community uses for patching, and it has a built-in test syntax: lines starting with ;` declare expected ROM bytes, and ;E>, ;W> and ;P> lines check user errors, warnings and prints. That lets a patch carry its own regression checks inside the assembly source.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage shows a GitHub Actions build badge and an r9.pm muncher badge for branch asar_19. The README.txt I fetched is served from a path labelled master_archived, which may mean the default branch was archived, but I could not confirm this from the pages. I did not find a last release date or last commit date in the pages I fetched. The online manual page I fetched is only a stub that points to the Asar 1.90 page and to a new Asar 2.0 manual.
brief.caveats: The README.txt describes Windows usage (double-clicking asar.exe), so Windows is the primary described platform; the build instructions cover Linux and Windows with Visual Studio. The documentation is split across README.txt, the online manual, and the changelog, and the online manual I fetched was only a redirect stub with no content. The test syntax section is written for contributors to the test suite. The README says a static library use requires an Asar-compatible licence, but it does not state the licence itself.

entry.title: asar
entry.tldr: An assembler for the Super Nintendo's 65c816, SPC700 and Super FX chips, used to patch existing ROMs or build new ones from assembly source.
entry.deeper_look:
Asar takes assembly source, called a patch file, plus a ROM image, and writes the assembled bytes into the ROM. It targets three SNES-era processors: the 65c816 main CPU, the SPC700 audio chip, and the Super FX coprocessor. It can also build a ROM from scratch. The README does not spell out exactly how output files are handled, so check the manual before trusting it with your only copy of anything.

It was created by Alcaro and modelled after xkas v0.06 by byuu, an older assembler from the same scene. The README describes it as a tool for SNES patching and ROM creation, and it is the assembler the ROM hacking community uses for this work.

The interesting idea is the patch as a small, surgical edit to someone else's program. You do not rebuild a game, you overwrite a few bytes at chosen addresses with new instructions. That is a way into 65816 assembly, memory maps, and how old cartridge software was laid out.

Asar also has a built-in test syntax. Lines starting with ;` declare the bytes expected in the ROM after patching, and ;E>, ;W> and ;P> lines check errors, warnings and prints. A patch can carry its own regression checks inside the assembly source. Asar can also be built as a DLL or static library for embedding in other tools.
entry.install:
brew install asar
# You also need your own SNES ROM image to patch. Prebuilt binaries are on the GitHub Releases page, or build from source with CMake.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the command-line usage. The README itself documents no command-line examples, so this is the quickest way to see the options.

entry.whats_unique: Patches can embed their own tests, with expected ROM bytes, errors, warnings and prints written as comments in the assembly source. It is also the assembler the SNES ROM hacking community actually uses.
entry.caveats: Project status is unclear (the README.txt path is labelled master_archived), the online manual is a stub pointing to other versions, and the docs mostly describe Windows usage.
